name: Eiffel Tower
short_description: Iconic iron lattice tower built for the 1889 World's Fair.

beats.script_body: The Eiffel Tower was designed not by Eiffel himself but by two engineers in his company, Koechlin and Nouguier, whose project won the competition for a striking monument for the 1889 Universal Exhibition. The Exhibition officially commemorated the centenary of the French Revolution — among competing proposals was a gigantic guillotine in honour of the victims of the Terror. Rising approximately 312 metres, the Tower was twice the height of the tallest structure previously built by man. Despite its gigantic dimensions, the iron structure weighed roughly 7,300 tonnes — an awesome technical feat. Yet on 7 May 1889, the day of its solemn inauguration, none of the lifts worked.
physical_cues: Four great iron legs tapering to the summit
beats.source_passage: Rising 318 metres above the ground, it was twice the height of the tallest construction hitherto ever built by man

beats.script_body: Not everyone welcomed the Tower. A petition signed by fifty leading figures from arts and letters — including Guy de Maupassant, Charles Gounod, Alexandre Dumas, and Charles Garnier — condemned the 'monstrous construction' in the name of Art and Civilisation. They showered it with metaphors: 'hollow candlestick', 'solitary riddled suppository', 'bald umbrella', 'skeleton'. Maupassant, contemplating leaving Paris, settled instead for lunching in the second-floor restaurant — the only spot in the city from which the Tower could not be seen. The painter Robert Delaunay saw it differently, making the Tower his favourite subject.
beats.source_passage: Guy de Maupassant, after an impulse to pack up and move out of the capital, decided instead to eat in the second-floor restaurant

beats.script_body: The Tower was meant to be ephemeral — a temporary structure for the World's Fair — and in 1909 enemies intensified campaigns to demolish it, claiming it was useless. Its salvation came from its height: wireless telegraphy was emerging, and the tall iron tower made a marvellous antenna. The first spoken news bulletin was broadcast from the Eiffel Tower in 1925, and in 1935 France's first experimental television transmission was made from here — a milestone that a few dozen excited enthusiasts received on their sets.
beats.source_passage: The first news bulletin was broadcast from the Eiffel Tower in 1925

beats.script_body: On 31 March 1889, the second anniversary of the beginning of construction, a sixty-strong party of top-hatted and monocled dignitaries made the first official ascent. Prime Minister Gustave Tirard gave up at the first floor; most of the others followed. But Gustave Eiffel persevered, urging the last ten breathless participants to the summit, where — with Paris spread at his feet — the Minister of Trade awarded him the Légion d'honneur. The honour, the book notes, should rightly have been shared with the two original designers, Koechlin and Nouguier.
beats.source_passage: On 31 March 1889, the second anniversary of the beginning of its construction

beats.script_body: The 1889 Universal Exhibition, and the Eiffel Tower at its heart, was not merely a celebration of engineering. The Third Republic, beleaguered by anarchists, revisionists and Boulangistes threatening its stability, organised the Exhibition to boost patriotic feeling and achieve political cohesion. It was to mark the Republic's recovery and trumpet France's entry into modernity — to dazzle the world and assert national prestige at a moment of profound internal vulnerability.
beats.source_passage: the Third Republic, beleaguered by anarchists, revisionists and Boulangistes

opening_hours_basis: Gated ticketed monument with elevator/stair access; hours follow the tower's own published year-round daily pattern (extended summer hours from mid-June).
visit_basis: The Champ de Mars and the space beneath the four piers absorb over half an hour of looking up and photographing; going up involves long security and lift queues plus two viewing levels and the summit, which would absorb well over two hours, capped at the 90-minute tour maximum.
judgement_basis: The Champ de Mars lawns run traffic-free but the immediate base is a fenced, security-controlled paved plaza crossed by roads and crowds where a child at speed can reach traffic and there is no quiet free seating; the site is brightly lit and busy with people at all hours, so a person left standing at night would be fine.
queue_basis: Airport-style security screening at the base perimeter plus separate lift-ticket lines feed a small number of elevators, so even timed tickets leave a substantial wait that worsens in summer midday, dropping only near opening or late evening.

anchors.label: The base
anchors.basis: The esplanade under the four feet is where the queues form and where a person stands to look straight up through the lattice; the corpus's queue and security lines are about this esplanade. Half the footprint, as a place you look at demands.

name: Quai Voltaire
short_description: Historic Left Bank embankment; Voltaire died at no. 27; Baudelaire, Wagner, Delacroix and Ingres all lived or worked here.

beats.script_body: Voltaire died at number 27 on 30 May 1778, aged 84. He had left the quai in 1723 finding it too noisy, but returned on 10 February 1778, and his host the Marquis de Villette gave him a room overlooking the quiet courtyard. When Voltaire's play Irène triumphed at the theatre, crowds pressed around his coach on the quai, then called quai des Théatins — named for the Order founded here by Mazarin in 1647. The Marquis illuminated the quai and replaced the street sign with a plaque reading quai Voltaire. Police removed it the next morning. The renaming only became official on 11 July 1791, when Voltaire's remains were transferred to the Panthéon.
beats.source_passage: where Voltaire died on 30 May 1778, at the age of 84

beats.script_body: The quai Voltaire reads like a roll-call of European culture. Delacroix lived at number 13 between 1829 and 1835, in a north-facing studio where the idea for his celebrated La Liberté Guidant le Peuple may have germinated. Corot came after; Ingres had a studio at number 17. Baudelaire lodged at number 19 between 1856 and 1858, working on Les Fleurs du Mal. Wagner completed Die Meistersinger here in the winter of 1861–62. Sibelius and Oscar Wilde also stayed at number 19. Alfred de Musset was at number 25 between 1839 and 1849.
physical_cues: Number 19 — hotel of Baudelaire, Wagner, Sibelius, Wilde
beats.source_passage: Between 1829 and 1835 Delacroix lived on the 5th floor at n° 13

beats.script_body: A mansion on the quai was occupied by Louise-Renée de Penacoët de Kéroualle, the artful mistress of Charles II of England, who used her charms to become Duchess of Portsmouth. Louis XIV valued her influence — it served his diplomatic dealings with England. When Charles II died, the Duchess removed as many works of art as she could carry from his magnificent collection and crammed them into her quai Voltaire residence.
physical_cues: Antique shops now occupying some of these buildings
beats.source_passage: Louise-Renée de Penacoét de Kéroualle, the artful mistress of Charles II

beats.script_body: The Hôtel de Tessé at number 1 was built on the site of a mansion that burned down in 1760 — along with its owner. The 80-year-old Marquis de Bacqueville had gone to the Opera knowing a fire had broken out in his house. When he returned and found it in flames, he walked back inside to rescue papers and never came out again. The same eccentric had, eighteen years earlier, fitted himself with two pairs of wings, launched from his rooftop, and attempted to fly across the Seine. His brief flight ended on a wash-shed on the river, and he with a broken leg.

At number 29, the Hôtel de Mailly-Nesle was home to five sisters, grand-daughters of the Duc de Mazarin. One by one they became mistresses of Louis XV — all but the third, kept under tight guard by her husband. The last, the Duchesse de Châteauroux, received an annual pension of 80,000 pounds from the royal lover. The mob called her 'La P... du Roi.' She died suddenly in 1744, aged only 27, in a first-floor room that still exists. By the following year, the Marquise de Pompadour had captured the King's heart.
beats.source_passage: Five delectable sisters, the grand-daughters of the Duc de Mazarin

opening_hours_basis: An open riverside embankment walked in the open air, gated by nothing.
visit_basis: Riverside embankment walked its length past 18th-century facades and plaques with open views across the Seine to the Louvre; a setting to stroll, nothing to enter.
judgement_basis: A Seine embankment street with a roadway and river parapets so children cannot safely run, no quiet free seating beside the traffic, but it is lit, open and central with people passing along the quay at night.
queue_basis: An open riverside embankment with no door or admission; the whole value stands in the open.

name: Fontaine des Quatre Saisons
short_description: Monumental 18th-century wall fountain at 57–59 rue de Grenelle, sculpted by Edme Bouchardon (1739–1745).

beats.script_body: Bouchardon's giant fountain, known as La Fontaine des Quatre Saisons, occupies numbers 57–59 rue de Grenelle. The four seasons are represented by chubby cupids — in spring flowers, harvesting, grape-picking (a frightened rabbit making a dash to escape), and sheltering under a blanket. Voltaire was unimpressed. He found the street too narrow for such an overbearing monument, and nicknamed it 'La Trompeuse' — the deceiver — because it contained 'so much stone for so little water.' There was some wisdom in the complaint: the fountains of Paris were supplied with filthy Seine water and contributed to cholera epidemics. The fountain is also literally deceptive: it is only a thin facing on a wall, a consequence of the nuns of the Recollettes refusing to surrender more than a narrow strip of their estate.
physical_cues: Massive stone facade towering over narrow street
beats.source_passage: Bouchardon's gigantic fountain known as La Fontaine des Quatre Saisons

opening_hours_basis: A monumental wall fountain on the street facade, viewed from the pavement at any hour.
visit_basis: Monumental Bouchardon wall fountain filling a street frontage with allegorical sculpture read across its full width; no interior.
judgement_basis: A monumental wall fountain set flush into buildings on the narrow rue de Grenelle, seen from the pavement beside traffic, with no free seating, no room to run, and a quiet dim street after dark.
queue_basis: A monumental wall fountain on a public street, viewed in the open with no gate or ticket.

name: Saint-Thomas-d'Aquin
short_description: 17th-century Dominican church on Place Saint-Thomas-d'Aquin, parish church of returning aristocratic émigrés after the Revolution.

beats.script_body: The church of Saint-Thomas-d'Aquin began as a Dominican noviciate, with its entrance on the now-demolished section of rue Saint-Dominique. Anne de Rohan-Montbazon, Duchesse de Luynes, laid the cornerstone on 5 March 1682. The Revolution dissolved the noviciate, but in 1804, when Christianity was no longer anathema, an enormous congregation gathered at the church's steps where Pope Pius VII gave them his blessing. It then became the parish church of the returning aristocratic émigrés of the Faubourg, their favourite place of worship.
beats.source_passage: Anne de Rohan-Montbazon, Duchesse de Luynes, was living at the Hétel de Luynes when she came over to lay the cornerstone

opening_hours_basis: A parish church you enter; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: 17th-century Dominican church with a classical facade on a small square; interior is a single broad nave with side chapels and a painted ceiling, about 15 minutes to walk through with no queue.
judgement_basis: A working church where quiet is expected so a child cannot run loose inside, no free public seating exists on its small paved place, but the square sits on lit central streets with people about after dark.
queue_basis: A parish church with an open door you walk straight through; there is no ticket desk or security screening to queue for.

name: Le Bon Marché
short_description: The world's first modern department store, founded 1838 at 24 rue de Sèvres; inspiration for Zola's Au Bonheur des Dames.

beats.script_body: In 1852, Aristide Boucicaut, a shop assistant at Au Petit Saint-Thomas on rue du Bac, was offered a partnership in a small hosiery shop, Au Bon Marché, at the corner of rue du Bac and rue de Sèvres. By 1863 he was its sole owner. Floor space grew from 30 square metres to 26,000 within sixty years. The extended premises used an iron structure involving Gustave Eiffel's firm (the 1872 expansion), the symbol of modernity. The story of Bon Marché is the story of triumphant capitalism — and Emile Zola explored its every mechanism to write his novel Au Bonheur des Dames.
physical_cues: Grand iron-and-glass building at 24 rue de Sèvres
beats.source_passage: new extended premises had an iron structure, the symbol of modernity, and were designed by Gustave Eiffel

beats.script_body: Emile Zola called the great department stores of Paris 'gigantic modern bazaars' and saw in them the engine of consumer society — destroying helpless small tradesmen in the process. The Bon Marché became the subject of his novel Au Bonheur des Dames: a world of sham, where the irresistible weapon of advertising lured the female client in, and where she was inevitably trapped, dazzled by overflowing goods and ever-changing fashions. Zola's relentless sociological mission was the exploration of how the machinery of 19th-century capitalism actually worked.
physical_cues: Overwhelming accumulation of goods on every floor
beats.source_passage: These gigantic 'modern bazaars', as Emile Zola called them

opening_hours_basis: A department store behind doors; hours from Le Bon Marché's own published store pattern.
visit_basis: Grand 19th-century department store with a famous iron-and-glass atrium, escalator well and multiple floors including the Grande Epicerie food hall; an engaged wander through the architecture and displays fills an hour.
judgement_basis: A department-store interior of fragile displays and paid café tables where children cannot run free and no free quiet seating exists, but rue de Sèvres outside is a busy lit street trafficked at night.
queue_basis: A department store with wide free-entry doors and no ticket or security line to enter; any waiting happens at checkout tills inside, not at the threshold.

name: La Pagode
short_description: Japanese-style pagoda cinema at 57 bis rue de Babylone, built 1895–96 by Alexandre Marcel; converted to cinema 1931.

beats.script_body: Down rue de Babylone at number 57 bis stands one of Paris's most extraordinary buildings: a pagoda-shaped structure built in 1895–96 by architect Alexandre Marcel — an authentic Frenchman despite the design — reportedly commissioned by a manager of the Bon Marché in an attempt to win back his unfaithful wife. Japonisme was the rage, which perhaps should have charmed Madame. The Chinese legation, who briefly rented the premises, moved out when they discovered murals inside celebrating Japan's victories over China. The building was converted into a cinema in 1931 and remains the only picture-house in the 7th arrondissement.
physical_cues: Pagoda roofline and Japanese architectural details

opening_hours_basis: A pagoda cinema you enter; gated, hours not confidently known (long closed for renovation); left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Ornate Japanese-style pagoda facade and garden gate viewed from the street; it is a working cinema, not an interior open to casual visiting, so nothing to enter as a tour stop.
judgement_basis: A cinema on a pavement offers no running room and no free seating, but rue de Babylone is a lit residential street with people passing after dark.
queue_basis: A neighbourhood cinema entered directly off the street; there is no standing queue to reach the building, only a box office for showtimes.
